metadata.text:
DIY CAMS OPERATION


KEEBLERKAM (ORIGINAL)
Characteristics:
	•	Body: Built from a large Keebler cracker tin.
	•	Lens: Very large magnifying lens, 6in diameter, 1in thick.
	•	Focal Length: Fixed at 112.5in.
	•	Aperture:
	•	Default: f/2.9 (4.5in diameter).
	•	With insert: f/8.7 (1.5in diameter).
	•	Additional lenses are insertable.
	•	Film Projection Area: 7.5in diameter circle (~38.5 sq in).
	•	Focus Distance: Fixed at ~33in from the subject.
Operational Parameters:
	•	ISO: ~80 (Fuji X-ray film).
	•	EV Range: Works best in EV 5–7.
	•	Exposure Times:
	•	At f/2.9: ~2–10 seconds depending on EV.
	•	At f/8.7: ~16–80 seconds depending on EV.
Strengths:
	•	Large projection area for wide and detailed compositions.
	•	Long exposures possible, especially with the reduced aperture.
Limitations:
	•	Fixed focus distance and aperture (unless modified).
	•	Requires precise subject placement at ~33in.
Original build: 7.5” dia Keebler soda cracker tin (silver interior, metallic Keebler-green branded exterior), ~5” dia orange 70s kitchen tin w/ stylized utensil outline pattern (in beige, cream, and maroon), 6” dia magnifying lens scavenged from estate facade, 4.5” dia cardboard oatmeal container, metal foil tape, black hand tape. Containers originally meant to be slideable to focus, later fixed due to construction constraints. Yellow anodized ring with 1” aperture was originally inserted stuck directly to lens w/ double sided foam tape w/ 3/4” gap all around, creating 
Current build: All of the original components, with changes—[see current specs]


CLAMPCAM
Characteristics:
	•	Body: Built from an adjustable bellows and a Minolta MD ROKKOR-X lens.
	•	Lens: 50mm f/2.0 Minolta lens (aperture adjustable from f/2.0 to f/16).
	•	Focal Length: Adjustable, ~3–7.5in (depends on bellows extension).
	•	Film Projection Area: 2.25 x 2.25in (~5 sq in).
	•	Focus Distance: Adjustable from 0.5m to infinity.
Operational Parameters:
	•	ISO: ~80 (Fuji X-ray film).
	•	EV Range: Works best in EV 5–7.
	•	Exposure Times:
	•	At f/2.0: ~0.3–1.2 seconds.
	•	At f/16: ~5–20 seconds.
With Additional Lens:
	•	Focal length and aperture recalibrate (needs testing).
	•	Likely increases magnification or narrows field of view.
Strengths:
	•	Flexible focus and aperture settings for creative control.
	•	Suitable for close-ups, precise compositions, and experimenting with depth of field.
Limitations:
	•	Small projection area limits the image size on film.
	•	Wide apertures (e.g., f/2.0) may struggle with sharpness on X-ray film.
General Observations
	•	KEEBLERKAM: Best for wide, stationary compositions with long exposures.
	•	CLAMPCAM: Ideal for detailed close-ups, variable focus, and shorter exposure times.
These summaries should serve as a good baseline for planning your shots! Let me know if you’d like a detailed table or further refinements.

THE ROYALE (ORIGINAL)
Camera Characteristics
	1.	Construction:
	•	Made from an antique wooden camera case with nested silver napkin rings.
	•	Focus achieved by sliding or flipping outer lens elements, and by moving the camera relative to the subject.
	2.	Optical Setup:
	•	Focal Length: ~9.25 in (~235 mm).
	•	Aperture Diameter: ~0.75 in (~19 mm).
	•	Aperture (f-number): Approx. f/12.
	3.	Film & Projection Area:
	•	Fuji X-ray film, ISO 100 assumed.
	•	Image area: ~3.5 x 4.25 in.
	4.	Focus Range:
	•	Focus possible from ~1 in to ~35 ft or farther (potentially infinity).
	5.	Shutter:
	•	No mechanical shutter; exposure controlled by flipping the light on/off.
	•	Minimum exposure: ~1/10 sec, with better precision in ~1/2 sec increments.
Operational Parameters
	1.	Lighting Conditions:
	•	Best suited for indoor lighting or controlled low-light environments.
	•	EV range: ~2–8 (dim to decently lit interiors).
	2.	Exposure Times (at f/12, ISO 100):
	•	Bright indoor lighting (EV 7): ~1 second.
	•	Typical indoor lighting (EV 6): ~2 seconds.
	•	Dim lighting (EV 4–5): ~4–8 seconds.
	•	Very dim lighting (EV 2–3): ~8–16 seconds or more.
	3.	Focusing:
	•	Depth of field is shallow at f/12, requiring careful focus adjustments by moving the camera relative to the subject.
	4.	Experimentation:
	•	Test exposures with bracketing (e.g., 1 sec, 2 sec, 4 sec) to account for film latitude and reciprocity failure.
	•	Adjust exposure based on observed results and lighting conditions.
Summary
The Royale operates as a fixed-aperture, large-format camera ideal for experimental photography in low-light, indoor conditions. Exposure times range from ~1–16 seconds depending on lighting, and focus requires precise manual adjustments. Bracketing and experimentation are key to success with this DIY setup.

metadata.name: KeeblerCam Lyon 373 Upgrades.txt
metadata.text:
KeeblerCam updates

Ok… latest updates to the KeeblerCam:

Put interior lens on rails (made of old folding ruler slats) with pull string to adjust. Slides in and out by about 3”, and flips… so, that gives me about 3” from front lens to about 6”. Also made a viewing hood made from a foam/nylon knee brace with a small picture frame and thick cardboard tube to hold it open, and a pitcher lid with a flip-top spout to view the screen through. Updated the belt harness for more motion control too (although still really only good for hanging positioning or arm strap)

metadata.name: Transparecam Prototype.txt
metadata.text:
Transparecam Prototype Specs & Speculation 


SPECS (original)

Here’s a consolidated Transparecam current full spec sheet (based on your working prototypes + the patent/concept documents), with the one exception of a non-transparent circular clamp added for holding/mounting:

⸻

📸 TRANSPARECAM — Current Full Specs

Core Body
	•	Main housing: Medium clear pill bottle (polypropylene, transparent orange)
	•	Film backplate insert: Smaller pill bottle, bottom cut off, inverted, slides inside medium bottle to hold film flat at correct focal distance
	•	Clamp: Circular band (metal or opaque plastic, external, non-transparent) for securing body to tripod, rig, or surface (added tolerance exception )

⸻

Optical
	•	Lens: ~2” diameter salvaged element
	•	Focal length: ~2.25” (≈ 57 mm)
	•	Aperture: Full diameter (≈ f/1.1)
	•	Alternate optics: Can swap in shorter FL lens for side-aperture panoramic builds

⸻

Film & Sensitivity
	•	Standard test stock: Blue-sensitive x-ray film (double-emulsion, orthochromatic)
	•	Nominal ISO: ~50–100 depending on exposure & reciprocity
	•	Other available emulsions: Ilford Pan F+ (ISO 50), Kodak T-MAX 100, Ilford Delta 3200 (usable with slower sweep) 
	•	Film loading: In dark or under rubylith envelope; circular cut film disks or strips taped to inner insert

⸻

Light Control
	•	Shutter methods:
	•	Lens cap / hand cover
	•	Rotatable rubylith sleeve lining inside bottle
	•	Pull-tab system (cut rubylith patch slides to uncover lens hole)
	•	Potential slit-sleeve + sweep (pull-string or rubber-band motor) for panoramas
	•	Ambient light safety: Rubylith tape (red, higher density) blocks daylight fogging; rubylith film (orange, semi-translucent) only partial protection 

⸻

Developer Integration
	•	Primary chemistry: Monobath (developer + fixer mix), inject with syringe post-exposure
	•	In-camera development: Developer fills interior chamber, image develops while visible through clear housing
	•	Options:
	•	Drain and rinse for archival negatives
	•	Retain developer (“snow globe mode”) for live art-object / display 

⸻

Exposure Metrics
	•	Indoor (bathroom light, ISO 50): ~1/18 s @ f/1.1
	•	Indoor (ISO 100): ~1/36 s @ f/1.1
	•	Night / moonlight canopy tests: Target sweep exposure per-point = 0.3–1.0 s (achieved with narrow slit + 8–16 s sweep rotation)
	•	Flash option: OPUS OPL-M100 Xenon (~100 Ws, quartz envelope → UV+VIS+IR) 

⸻

Variants (Modular Concepts)
	•	Dual exposure: Two lenses (front + side), rubylith rotation covers one while exposing other
	•	Panoramic: Inner barrel rotation sweeps a narrow slit across film plane (string-pull or rubber-band wind-up)
	•	Educational: Film doubles as translucent “ground glass” for live viewing before exposure 
	•	Snow globe: Retain liquid developer around film for display 

⸻

✅ Key Rule: All visible structure transparent/translucent, except holding clamp. Emphasis is on proof-of-concept and spectacle (visible image formation), not photographic fidelity .

⸻

Do you want me to also diagram the current build schematic (side cutaway with labeled parts: lens, rubylith sleeve, film insert, clamp, injection port), so you’ve got a visual reference for documentation/pitch?
============
USE

Totally—think of it this way:

How dark for ~1 second at f/1.1

At ISO 100, 1 s @ f/1.1 corresponds to about EV ≈ 0.3.
At ISO 50, it’s EV ≈ –0.7.
That’s very dim—roughly “dark hallway / very dim room with a single distant lamp.”

From your bathroom reading (~1/18 s @ f/1.1, ISO 50), to reach 1 s you need about +4½–5½ stops less light (dimmer room, farther lamp, or transparent ND/smoked acrylic over the light).

Did you just make a transparent low-light camera?

Pretty much, yes. Wide-open at f/1.1, ortho (x-ray) film + your rubylith body can record scenes in very low light if you can hold ½–2 s (or longer) exposures steady.

Should you shoot the moon? Graveyards at night?
	•	The moon itself (the bright disc): it’s sunlit rock—very bright. Using the “Looney 11” equivalent, you’d need around 1/10,000 s @ f/1.1, ISO 100 (≈1/5,000 s @ ISO 50). You don’t have that shutter control, so the moon will blow out unless you add transparent ND or a smaller clear aperture.
	•	Moonlit landscapes / graveyards (no artificial lights): average scene brightness ≈ EV −3 to −1. With your camera that’s on the order of 4–30 s @ f/1.1, ISO 50–100 (then add ½–1½ stops for reciprocity). That’s very doable if you can keep it steady.
	•	Graveyard with path lights / porch lamps: typically EV 0–2 → you’ll be in the ½–4 s zone at f/1.1, ISO 50. Also doable.

How to hit 1 s without breaking “no opacity”
	•	Make the scene dimmer: back the lamp way up, bounce it off a wall/ceiling, crack a door, or shoot in a darker room.
	•	Use transparent attenuation: a sheet of smoked/gray-tinted acrylic (ND) over the room light or over the lens. Still visibly transparent.
	•	Use a smaller clear aperture: a transparent disc with a clean round clear hole (no black stop). Smaller clear hole = longer time, still “see-through.”

Quick starting guide
	•	1 s goal (ISO 50): aim for a very dim room (EV ~−1) or use transparent ND to cut light by ~5 stops from your bathroom baseline.
	•	Moonlit yard: try 8–20 s @ f/1.1 (ISO 50); bracket ×2 and ×4 for reciprocity.
	•	Path-lit graveyard: start 1–4 s @ f/1.1 (ISO 50); bracket ½–8 s.

Steady support helps a ton—brace the bottle against a railing/tree or plop it on a stable surface. If you want, I can give you a tiny EV→time cheat card tuned to f/1.1 and ISO 50/100 so you can pick times on the fly.

=========
USE RECOMMENDATIONS

Good way to frame it. With x-ray film (orthochromatic, slow, fairly forgiving in terms of getting an image but not forgiving for tonal accuracy), here’s what “tolerance” looks like in practice:

⸻

⚖️ Exposure tolerance (ballpark for ISO 50 stock)
	•	Within ±1 stop → Very usable image, printable/scan-able.
	•	Within ±2 stops → Still an image, but thin (under) or dense (over). Proof-of-concept success.
	•	Beyond ±3 stops →
• Overexposed: film base goes nearly opaque, highlights block up, but you’ll still see something.
• Underexposed: film looks faint/ghostly; after monobath you may see a weak outline, but detail is gone.

👉 For your purpose: ±2 stops is totally “in bounds.” You don’t have to nail it.

⸻

💡 Translate to your bathroom reading
	•	Meter says ~1/18 s at ISO 50, f/1.1.
	•	One stop either way = 1/9 s or 1/36 s.
	•	Two stops either way = 1/4.5 s or 1/72 s.

So your proof-of-concept window is roughly 1/5 s to 1/70 s. Anything in that zone should give you some image.

⸻

🎞️ Development tolerance (monobath)
	•	Monobaths tend to compress contrast, which actually helps here.
	•	Leaving the film in 1–2× longer than “ideal” usually just gives you denser negatives, but not blanks.
	•	Too short a time = weak image, but still visible.

⸻

✅ Bottom line:
If your hand-flick lands anywhere between about 1/5 and 1/70 s, you’ll get a proof image. That’s a very generous margin. Perfect exposure isn’t needed — you just want silver halide reduction to prove the transparent-camera + in-camera dev concept.

⸻

Do you want me to also give you a quick “cheat scale” (time ranges per stop around your reading) you can tape to the bottle so you don’t have to think about it mid-experiment?

Right — I understand your intent from your README : you want within tolerance, not perfection, and with the constraint that the build stays fully transparent.

⸻

To slow your f/1.1 pill-bottle cam to ~1 second:

1. Exposure math baseline
	•	Your bathroom test gave ~1/18 s @ ISO 50, f/1.1.
	•	To stretch that to ~1 s, you need about 5½ stops less light.

⸻

2. Transparent-friendly ways to cut ~5–6 stops

Since “no opacity” is the rule:
	•	Rubylith attenuator layers
Stack 2–3 layers of rubylith in front of the lens. Each layer behaves roughly like a strong red filter: it blocks most of the film-sensitive blue/green, so effective speed drops dramatically.
You’ll need to test, but expect 2–3 layers to easily buy 4–6 stops.
	•	Neutral-density (ND) acrylic / smoked acrylic
Available as see-through gray plastic (still visibly transparent). A piece over the lens can give you –3, –6, or even –9 stops depending on grade.
	•	Distance from light
Every doubling of distance = –2 stops. If your bathroom bulb is 1 m away, moving to ~3 m distance already slows things down 4–5×. Combine with a single rubylith sheet and you’re near 1 s.

⸻

3. Tolerance window
	•	At f/1.1, ISO 50, in your bathroom lighting:
	•	1/18 s = “metered”
	•	1/9 s to 1/36 s = ±1 stop → still good
	•	1/4 s to 1/72 s = ±2 stops → proof-of-concept usable
	•	So if you manage to stretch into the ½–2 s range, reciprocity failure of x-ray film actually makes it easier (the film “slows down” at long exposures).

⸻

✅ Answer: To hit ~1 second, you need to cut light by ~5–6 stops. That’s achievable with 2–3 layers of rubylith, a smoked/ND acrylic disc, or simply moving the light source farther away. All of these keep the system fully transparent.

⸻

Would you like me to draft a quick table: “How many rubylith layers ≈ how many stops” so you can just pick the combo to hit ~1 s without trial-and-error?

Right — now you’re in the “transparent camera = instant darkroom” stage. Here’s what happens once you close the cap and inject the monobath:

⸻

🔄 Step-by-step, in your pill-bottle cam (ISO 50 x-ray film, “underleaf” scene)
	1.	Exposure is made
	•	Lens cap off for your timed “underleaf” exposure.
	•	Cap goes back on = film is no longer receiving light.
	2.	Developer hits emulsion
	•	You inject monobath through a port or syringe hole.
	•	The liquid flows around the film’s surface, wetting it evenly.
	•	The developing agents (Metol/Hydroquinone/Phenidone etc.) start reducing the exposed silver halide crystals to metallic silver (the black image).
	3.	Fixing happens at the same time
	•	In a monobath, the fixer (thiosulfate) is present too.
	•	It dissolves the unexposed silver halide crystals while the developers are working on the exposed ones.
	•	The balance is: development happens fast on exposed grains, while unexposed ones dissolve away more slowly.
	4.	The image appears before your eyes ✨
	•	Within 30–60 seconds, you’ll start to see darker areas form on the film base.
	•	By 2–3 minutes, most of the visible image density is there.
	•	By 5–6 minutes, it’s “done enough” to rinse or leave as-is (depending on your monobath recipe).
	5.	Spectacle of transparency
	•	Because the camera body is rubylith/amber and the film itself is translucent, you can watch the negative image bloom in real time through the camera walls.
	•	Highlights (leaf gaps, sky patches) → go clear.
	•	Shadows (leaf veins, tree silhouettes) → go dark.
	•	It’s like a Polaroid + lava lamp hybrid.

⸻

🧪 Practical notes
	•	Agitation: gently swirl or tilt the pill-bottle to spread chemistry evenly. The rubylith glow makes the developer swirl look dramatic.
	•	Air bubbles: a couple will cling, making tiny undeveloped spots — part of the “lava lamp” aesthetic.
	•	Retention vs. drain:
	•	If you keep the monobath inside → you get the “snow globe” display version.
	•	If you drain after ~5 min → you’ll have a clearer negative that’s easier to scan.

⸻

✅ So with the current ISO 50 x-ray setup:
	•	Cap off → ½–2 s underleaf exposure
	•	Cap on → inject monobath
	•	Watch it develop through red bottle walls for ~3–6 minutes
	•	End result: a translucent negative, still viewable in-camera or removable for scanning.

⸻

Do you want me to sketch a timeline diagram (0–6 minutes) showing what the image looks like as it develops in real time inside the transparent body?

Right — now you’re in the “transparent camera = instant darkroom” stage. Here’s what happens once you close the cap and inject the monobath:

⸻

🔄 Step-by-step, in your pill-bottle cam (ISO 50 x-ray film, “underleaf” scene)
	1.	Exposure is made
	•	Lens cap off for your timed “underleaf” exposure.
	•	Cap goes back on = film is no longer receiving light.
	2.	Developer hits emulsion
	•	You inject monobath through a port or syringe hole.
	•	The liquid flows around the film’s surface, wetting it evenly.
	•	The developing agents (Metol/Hydroquinone/Phenidone etc.) start reducing the exposed silver halide crystals to metallic silver (the black image).
	3.	Fixing happens at the same time

	•	It dissolves the unexposed silver halide crystals while the developers are working on the exposed ones.
	•	The balance is: development happens fast on exposed grains, while unexposed ones dissolve away more slowly.
	4.	The image appears before your eyes ✨
	•	Within 30–60 seconds, you’ll start to see darker areas form on the film base.
	•	By 2–3 minutes, most of the visible image density is there.
	•	By 5–6 minutes, it’s “done enough” to rinse or leave as-is (depending on your monobath recipe).
	5.	Spectacle of transparency
	•	Because the camera body is rubylith/amber and the film itself is translucent, you can watch the negative image bloom in real time through the camera walls.
	•	Highlights (leaf gaps, sky patches) → go clear.
	•	Shadows (leaf veins, tree silhouettes) → go dark.
	•	It’s like a Polaroid + lava lamp hybrid.

⸻

🧪 Practical notes
	•	Agitation: gently swirl or tilt the pill-bottle to spread chemistry evenly. The rubylith glow makes the developer swirl look dramatic.
	•	Air bubbles: a couple will cling, making tiny undeveloped spots — part of the “lava lamp” aesthetic.
	•	Retention vs. drain:
	•	If you keep the monobath inside → you get the “snow globe” display version.
	•	If you drain after ~5 min → you’ll have a clearer negative that’s easier to scan.

⸻

✅ So with the current ISO 50 x-ray setup:
	•	Cap off → ½–2 s underleaf exposure
	•	Cap on → inject monobath
	•	Watch it develop through red bottle walls for ~3–6 minutes
	•	End result: a translucent negative, still viewable in-camera or removable for scanning.

⸻

Do you want me to sketch a timeline diagram (0–6 minutes) showing what the image looks like as it develops in real time inside the transparent body?

Exactly ✅

That’s the whole magic of your transparent rubylith-lined body + x-ray film + monobath concept:
	•	During exposure → the cap is off, so the film sees blue/green light through the lens.
	•	Cap goes back on → the rubylith lining + cap block the wavelengths x-ray film is sensitive to (≈350–550 nm). To your eyes it’s still glowing orange/red, but to the film it’s effectively dark.
	•	Developer injected → now the only action is the chemistry, not the light.
	•	Bring it into a normal lit room → no problem, because the film is shielded by rubylith. You and anyone else can literally watch the silver image appear in broad room light.

That was the “hook” all along in the Transparecam notes  : a daylight-safe, visibly transparent camera where you see the image bloom into existence in real time.

⸻

⚡ One caution:
	•	Thin rubylith = safer indoors than out. In bright sun, some blue/green can leak through thin areas or seams and slowly fog. Inside with standard household lighting (mostly warm LEDs/incandescents), you’re safe to watch the whole 3–6 min process.

⸻

Would you like me to lay out a step-by-step demo script (expose → cap → inject → bring inside → watch → rinse/drain) that you could literally use to show this off to someone on video?

=========
UPGRADE IDEAS 

Bingo — you’ve just boiled the workflow down to its simplest, most show-stopping form:

⸻

🌌 Transparecam “Processor” Workflow
	1.	Expose
	•	Take your pill-bottle Transparecam outside at night.
	•	Aim it at tree leaves, moonlight, a lamplit graveyard — anything with contrast.
	•	Do a nice, slow exposure (½ s → 30 s, depending on scene).
	•	Cover the lens with the cap again (or just seal it and drop it in the dark bag).
	2.	Secure
	•	Transport back indoors.
	•	As long as the cap stays on and the rubylith liner is intact, the film is protected.
	3.	Process in full light
	•	Sit down in your kitchen or bathroom with the lights on.
	•	Inject monobath through the port/syringe hole.
	•	Tilt/swirl gently.
	4.	Watch the fireworks ✨
	•	Within 30–60 s: faint shapes bloom on the translucent film.
	•	2–3 min: image density builds — shadows darken, highlights clear.
	•	5–6 min: development is effectively done.
	•	You’ve literally watched the photo form in the transparent camera.
	5.	Aftermath
	•	Drain if you want a clean negative to scan.
	•	Or leave the liquid inside — snow-globe style — as a permanent art object/display.

⸻

✅ So yes: the “processor” is just night exposure + cover → carry inside → inject → watch.
That’s the exact moment people will freak out about — not just the picture, but the fact they see it happen.

⸻

Do you want me to write up a demo script (like a short performance flow) you could follow if you want to film or show this process live to someone?

Yes 👏 — you’ve just hit on the rotary multi-exposure version of Transparecam. Think of it as a “see-through TLR / turret” where film wraps around a curved surface and rubylith acts as both safelight and shutter.

⸻

🔄 Concept: Dual-Lens Rotational Exposure Camera

Structure
	•	Outer bottle = transparent shell, with two clear optical ports (front + side).
	•	Inner bottle = film carrier cylinder, rubylith-lined, rotates inside outer bottle.
	•	Film = wrapped around inner cylinder (curved film plane).
	•	Lens A (front) and Lens B (side) each have their own rubylith “shutter windows.”

Operation
	1.	First exposure (front lens):
	•	Rotate inner cylinder so clear window aligns with Lens A.
	•	Film behind Lens A gets exposed.
	•	As you continue rotating, that same section of film is carried under a rubylith patch (safe again).
	2.	Second exposure (side lens):
	•	Keep rotating until clear window aligns with Lens B.
	•	Rubylith automatically slides in front of the Lens A section (so the first image is protected).
	•	Film at the side port is now exposed through Lens B.
	3.	After exposures:
	•	Whole inner cylinder is rotated into “locked/safe” mode (all windows covered with rubylith).
	•	Camera can then be developed transparently.

⸻

🧩 Engineering trick
	•	Rubylith “sleeve” system:
	•	Attach rubylith flaps or cutouts to the inner rotating cylinder.
	•	As you rotate, one window opens while the other closes.
	•	Think of a revolver cylinder or a rotating darkslide.
	•	Indexing:
	•	Mark simple detents at “Lens A open” and “Lens B open.”
	•	Each click = one exposure, with the other automatically blocked.

⸻

🌌 Creative potential
	•	Two perspectives in one development:
	•	One image forward, one image sideways — surreal compositions on the same strip.
	•	Both negatives develop together in monobath → you see the dual image bloom at once.
	•	Variations:
	•	More lenses/ports (triangular “fishbowl” exposures).
	•	Overlap exposures intentionally for composite art.
	•	Rotate partway for slit-scan-like streaks.

⸻

⚠️ Challenges
	•	Film flatness: curved base can distort sharpness with normal lenses, but small apertures (or pinholes) will tolerate it.
	•	Rubylith precision: must cover each exposed section tightly, otherwise stray light veils the earlier exposure.
	•	Light leaks at seams: since you’re rotating transparent parts, you’ll want tongue-and-groove style overlaps (transparent but labyrinthine).

⸻

✅ Bottom line:
You can absolutely design a rotating dual-lens transparecam where turning the cylinder both makes a new exposure and rubylith-covers the old one. It becomes a kind of see-through multi-shot camera with a built-in safelight shutter system.

⸻

Would you like me to draw a schematic cross-section showing outer shell, rotating rubylith sleeve, and how Lens A gets blocked when Lens B opens (and vice versa)? That would make the mechanism much clearer.

Oh yeah—you can turn your rotating-bottle rig into a true panoramic / slit-scan camera while keeping everything visibly transparent. Here’s a build that works with your “no opacity” rule (rubylith acts as the mask; the slit itself is clear).

Panoramic “rotary barrel” concept
	•	Film: wrapped around the inner cylinder (your small pill bottle) = naturally curved film plane (perfect for panoramas).
	•	Lens: fixed on the outer shell.
	•	Shutter/Aperture: a vertical clear slit in a rubylith sleeve that rotates relative to the lens. As the slit sweeps across, each point on the film gets a brief exposure. Everything else stays rubylith-red (safe), so the whole camera remains see-through.

You can do it either way:
	•	Rotate the inner film cylinder behind a fixed clear slit, or
	•	Rotate a rubylith slit sleeve in front of a stationary film cylinder.
Pick whichever is easier to fabricate; the math below is the same as long as the slit moves relative to the film.

⸻

How the exposure works (simple, reliable math)

For cylindrical panoramas, set the film radius roughly equal to the lens focal length (R ≈ f) so infinity focus tracks well during the sweep. With your lens f ≈ 57 mm:

Per-point exposure time (how long any spot on the film is uncovered):
t \;\approx\; \frac{w}{\omega\,f}
	•	w = slit width on the film (mm)
	•	\omega = rotation speed (radians/s) of the slit relative to the film
	•	f = focal length (mm)

Worked examples (with f = 57 mm)
	•	Want ~1 s per point with a 1 mm slit →
\omega \approx \frac{1}{t\,f} = \frac{1}{1 \times 57} \approx 0.0175\ \text{rad/s} \approx 1^\circ/s.
(A leisurely hand turn.)
	•	Want ~1/5 s per point with 1 mm slit →
\omega \approx \frac{1}{0.2 \times 57} \approx 0.087\ \text{rad/s} \approx 5^\circ/s.
	•	Keep your rotation speed comfortable (say 1–5°/s) and just pick w to land the time you want:
	•	\omega = 1^\circ/s (~0.0175 rad/s) → w ≈ 1 mm → t ≈ 1 s, w ≈ 0.5 mm → t ≈ 0.5 s
	•	\omega = 5^\circ/s (~0.087 rad/s) → w ≈ 1 mm → t ≈ 0.2 s

Tip: make two or three slit widths (e.g., 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 mm) on the same rotating rubylith sleeve; just index to the one you want.

⸻

Field of view & sweep
	•	Pan angle = how far you rotate. 120°–180° is easy by hand.
	•	Vertical image height = the clear vertical height of your slit (on the film). Make it, say, 15–20 mm tall to match your film strip height.
	•	Because the film is curved at R ≈ f, straight verticals near the center stay straight, classic swing-lens look.

⸻

Build steps (transparent only)
	1.	Film cylinder (inner bottle)
	•	Wrap your film emulsion-out around the inner bottle. Use clear retainer bands or a transparent collar to keep it flat. (No black anything.)
	•	Keep the rubylith liner continuous behind all non-imaging areas so the film stays safe.
	2.	Lens on outer bottle
	•	Mount your 57 mm lens to the outer shell mouth as you did before.
	3.	Rotating slit sleeve (rubylith)
	•	Make a rubylith band that fits around the inner cylinder (or around the outer, your choice).
	•	Cut a straight vertical clear slit (e.g., 1.0 mm wide × 18 mm tall).
	•	Add 1–2 more slits of different widths on the same band (spaced around the circumference).
	•	All non-slit area remains rubylith = visibly transparent red = light-safe for ortho film.
	4.	Indexing
	•	Mark two or three detents (tiny clear dots you can see through) so you can start the sweep at a known angle and stop at “closed” safely.
	5.	Seal, but stay transparent
	•	At the seam between rotating parts, use clear tongue-and-groove geometry (overlap the plastics) for a labyrinth path; no black foam. The rubylith itself provides the safelight block.

⸻

Shooting workflow (night / dim scenes)
	1.	Compose / aim (cap on is okay; you’ll be doing a sweep).
	2.	Start position: align the slit just before it reaches the lens axis (closed).
	3.	Open & sweep: remove cap (if used), begin rotating smoothly at ~1–5°/s through your desired pan angle.
	4.	Finish: rotate to “closed” (rubylith in front of frame again).
	5.	Process: inject monobath and watch the panorama bloom in the bottle.

⸻

Practical targets for your ISO 50 x-ray film
	•	Under leaves / dim room with lamp: aim t ≈ 0.5–2 s per point. Choose slit/rotation accordingly (see examples).
	•	Moonlit yard: you’ll likely want 1–10 s per point → go slower (1°/s) and/or narrow the slit (0.5 mm).
	•	Path-lit graveyard: 0.2–1 s per point works; 1 mm slit at 3–5°/s is in range.

Reciprocity at multi-second times gives you extra forgiveness; err slightly long.

⸻

Troubleshooting (transparent-only tricks)
	•	Veiling / low contrast: increase rubylith density around all non-slit areas; keep slit edges clean and straight. A tiny clear collar right behind the lens (like a transparent tube) helps confine rays to the slit path without opacity.
	•	Banding: rotation speed uneven—practice a constant sweep; add a light clear flywheel ring to smooth your hand.
	•	Softness: make the slit narrower (shorter per-point exposure → less smear), or rotate slower to match your time goal.

⸻

If you want, I can draft a one-page diagram showing: lens, curved film at R ≈ f, the rotating rubylith slit sleeve, slit widths, and arrows for rotation—with a little table that maps slit width + rotation speed → per-point exposure for your 57 mm lens.

Absolutely—let’s put numbers on a rubber-band wind-up panoramic sweep and translate it to exposure per point with your 57 mm lens.

How the exposure works (one clean formula)

For a rotating slit camera, the time any spot on the film is uncovered is:
t \;=\; \frac{w}{\omega\,f} \;=\; \frac{w\,T}{f\,\theta}
	•	w = slit width on the film (mm)
	•	\omega = angular speed (radians/s)
	•	f = focal length (mm) — you: 57 mm
	•	T = total sweep time (s)
	•	\theta = total sweep angle (radians) — e.g., 180° = \pi rad

This is handy because with a rubber band you’ll think in “how far” (θ) and “how long” (T).

What a rubber band motor gives you
	•	Wrap a clear/silicone band on a clear spindle attached to your rotating sleeve.
	•	Wind 1–3 turns, then release.
	•	Add a clear flywheel disk on the same axle to smooth speed (highly recommended).
	•	Use transparent stops (nubs/slots) to limit the sweep to, say, 10°–180°.

Average angular speed for a controlled sweep is \omega \approx \theta/T. With the flywheel, this stays fairly constant.

Pick your sweep & slit, then read off the per-point exposure

(Using your f = 57 mm. Times in seconds.)

A) Big panorama (θ = 180°)

Great for wide scenes, but each point gets a short exposure unless the sweep is very slow.

Sweep time T	w = 0.5 mm	1.0 mm	2.0 mm
2 s	0.006	0.011	0.022
4 s	0.011	0.022	0.045
8 s	0.022	0.045	0.089
16 s	0.045	0.089	0.179

👉 For dim night scenes on ISO 50, those per-point times are usually too short unless your scene is fairly bright.

B) Moderate swing (θ = 30°)

Nice compromise: still panoramic feel, longer per-point times.

T	0.5 mm	1.0 mm	2.0 mm
2 s	0.034	0.067	0.134
4 s	0.067	0.134	0.268
8 s	0.134	0.268	0.536
16 s	0.268	0.536	1.072

C) Tight sweep (θ = 20° … 10°)

Use this near the lens axis for slow scenes (moonlit leaves, path-lit trees).

20° sweep
	•	8 s with 1.0 mm slit → 0.402 s per point
	•	16 s with 1.0 mm slit → 0.804 s per point

10° sweep
	•	8 s with 1.0 mm slit → 0.804 s per point
	•	16 s with 1.0 mm slit → 1.608 s per point

Rule of thumb: to get into the ½–1.5 s per-point sweet spot for ISO 50 night scenes, use a small sweep angle (10–20°) and a multi-second sweep time (8–16 s) with a ~1 mm slit.

How to build/calibrate the wind-up
	•	Spindle & band: 8–12 mm diameter clear spindle; one wind = one turn (~360°).
	•	Stops: cut transparent detents so the sleeve travels exactly 10°, 20°, 30°, or 180°.
	•	Flywheel: clear acrylic disk (30–50 mm ⌀) on the axle—dramatically smooths speed.
	•	Speed check: put a tiny clear dot on the rotating part; film a test sweep on your phone and count frames → you’ll know T precisely.
	•	Index slits: put 0.5/1/2 mm slits on the same sleeve at different azimuths; wind to the mark you want.

Practical exposure tips (ISO 50 x-ray, night)
	•	Leaf canopy with moon/lamps: aim 0.3–1.0 s per point. Start with 20° in 8–12 s, 1 mm slit.
	•	Path-lit graveyard: 0.2–0.6 s per point is often enough → 30° in 4–8 s, 1 mm slit.
	•	Add ½–1 stop extra for reciprocity once you’re around 1 s per point (err long).
	•	After the sweep, rotate to rubylith-closed, go inside, inject monobath, and enjoy the show.

If you want, tell me your target sweep angle and how many seconds your rubber band can deliver comfortably; I’ll spit back the slit width that lands you in the right exposure zone.

metadata.text:
DIY CAM SIMULTANEOUS EXPOSURE

Choosing the Right EV and Exposure Time
	•	Target EV: EV 6 is a solid middle ground for indoor lighting. This allows moderate exposure times across all cameras without excessive risk of reciprocity failure (common with X-ray film).
	•	Exposure Time: Aim for 4 seconds, as this aligns reasonably well with all three cameras at their most workable aperture settings.

Per-Camera Settings
KEEBLERKAM
	•	Aperture: Use f/2.9 to minimize exposure time. This aperture gives enough light for EV 6 at ~4 seconds without the need for the longer exposures required by f/8.7.
	•	Focus: Ensure the subject is 33 inches away, as focus is fixed.
	•	Projection Area: Double-check film placement and backing to avoid light leaks, given the larger projection area.
CLAMPCAM
	•	Aperture: Set to f/4.0, which balances light-gathering capability with reasonable depth of field. This aperture matches well with KEEBLERKAM’s f/2.9 exposure time for EV 6.
	•	Focus: Adjust the bellows for precise focusing at the same distance (e.g., ~33 inches or closer for detailed shots).
	•	Projection Area: Ensure the film is flat and securely clamped.
THE ROYALE
	•	Aperture: Fixed at f/12.
	•	Focus: Carefully adjust the camera’s position to focus on the subject at the same distance as the other cameras.
	•	Exposure: At f/12 and EV 6, a 4-second exposure will work, though it might be slightly underexposed. X-ray film's latitude can compensate.

Film Development
	•	Contrast Control: X-ray film tends to have high contrast, which you can moderate during development. Use a diluted developer (e.g., 1:1 or 1:2 dilution for standard developers) and monitor closely.
	•	Development Time: Start with shorter times (e.g., ~5–6 minutes) and adjust based on initial tests.
	•	Agitation: Use gentle, consistent agitation to avoid uneven development, particularly for the larger sheets.

Practical Tips
	1.	Test Exposure Once: Before committing to a full run with all three cameras, do a single test exposure with one camera (e.g., The Royale) using your planned 4-second exposure at EV 6.
	2.	Lighting Consistency: Use a stable, repeatable light source to eliminate variability.
	3.	Film Placement: Double-check film placement and backing material for all cameras to prevent light leaks or uneven exposure.

Why 4 Seconds?
	•	It’s short enough to accommodate The Royale's f/12 aperture at EV 6.
	•	KEEBLERKAM and CLAMPCAM can adjust their apertures to match this time while staying within reasonable depth of field limits.
	•	It avoids the need for long exposure times that could exacerbate X-ray film's reciprocity failure.
By maintaining consistent exposure settings, using EV 6 lighting, and carefully controlling development, you should be able to capture usable and comparable images across all three cameras.

Transparecam Prototype Specs & Speculation 


SPECS (original)

Here’s a consolidated Transparecam current full spec sheet (based on your working prototypes + the patent/concept documents), with the one exception of a non-transparent circular clamp added for holding/mounting:

⸻

📸 TRANSPARECAM — Current Full Specs

Core Body
	•	Main housing: Medium clear pill bottle (polypropylene, transparent orange)
	•	Film backplate insert: Smaller pill bottle, bottom cut off, inverted, slides inside medium bottle to hold film flat at correct focal distance
	•	Clamp: Circular band (metal or opaque plastic, external, non-transparent) for securing body to tripod, rig, or surface (added tolerance exception )

⸻

Optical
	•	Lens: ~2” diameter salvaged element
	•	Focal length: ~2.25” (≈ 57 mm)
	•	Aperture: Full diameter (≈ f/1.1)
	•	Alternate optics: Can swap in shorter FL lens for side-aperture panoramic builds

⸻

Film & Sensitivity
	•	Standard test stock: Blue-sensitive x-ray film (double-emulsion, orthochromatic)
	•	Nominal ISO: ~50–100 depending on exposure & reciprocity
	•	Other available emulsions: Ilford Pan F+ (ISO 50), Kodak T-MAX 100, Ilford Delta 3200 (usable with slower sweep) 
	•	Film loading: In dark or under rubylith envelope; circular cut film disks or strips taped to inner insert

⸻

Light Control
	•	Shutter methods:
	•	Lens cap / hand cover
	•	Rotatable rubylith sleeve lining inside bottle
	•	Pull-tab system (cut rubylith patch slides to uncover lens hole)
	•	Potential slit-sleeve + sweep (pull-string or rubber-band motor) for panoramas
	•	Ambient light safety: Rubylith tape (red, higher density) blocks daylight fogging; rubylith film (orange, semi-translucent) only partial protection 

⸻

Developer Integration
	•	Primary chemistry: Monobath (developer + fixer mix), inject with syringe post-exposure
	•	In-camera development: Developer fills interior chamber, image develops while visible through clear housing
	•	Options:
	•	Drain and rinse for archival negatives
	•	Retain developer (“snow globe mode”) for live art-object / display 

⸻

Exposure Metrics
	•	Indoor (bathroom light, ISO 50): ~1/18 s @ f/1.1
	•	Indoor (ISO 100): ~1/36 s @ f/1.1
	•	Night / moonlight canopy tests: Target sweep exposure per-point = 0.3–1.0 s (achieved with narrow slit + 8–16 s sweep rotation)
	•	Flash option: OPUS OPL-M100 Xenon (~100 Ws, quartz envelope → UV+VIS+IR) 

⸻

Variants (Modular Concepts)
	•	Dual exposure: Two lenses (front + side), rubylith rotation covers one while exposing other
	•	Panoramic: Inner barrel rotation sweeps a narrow slit across film plane (string-pull or rubber-band wind-up)
	•	Educational: Film doubles as translucent “ground glass” for live viewing before exposure 
	•	Snow globe: Retain liquid developer around film for display 

⸻

✅ Key Rule: All visible structure transparent/translucent, except holding clamp. Emphasis is on proof-of-concept and spectacle (visible image formation), not photographic fidelity .

⸻

Do you want me to also diagram the current build schematic (side cutaway with labeled parts: lens, rubylith sleeve, film insert, clamp, injection port), so you’ve got a visual reference for documentation/pitch?
============
USE

Totally—think of it this way:

How dark for ~1 second at f/1.1

At ISO 100, 1 s @ f/1.1 corresponds to about EV ≈ 0.3.
At ISO 50, it’s EV ≈ –0.7.
That’s very dim—roughly “dark hallway / very dim room with a single distant lamp.”

From your bathroom reading (~1/18 s @ f/1.1, ISO 50), to reach 1 s you need about +4½–5½ stops less light (dimmer room, farther lamp, or transparent ND/smoked acrylic over the light).

Did you just make a transparent low-light camera?

Pretty much, yes. Wide-open at f/1.1, ortho (x-ray) film + your rubylith body can record scenes in very low light if you can hold ½–2 s (or longer) exposures steady.

Should you shoot the moon? Graveyards at night?
	•	The moon itself (the bright disc): it’s sunlit rock—very bright. Using the “Looney 11” equivalent, you’d need around 1/10,000 s @ f/1.1, ISO 100 (≈1/5,000 s @ ISO 50). You don’t have that shutter control, so the moon will blow out unless you add transparent ND or a smaller clear aperture.
	•	Moonlit landscapes / graveyards (no artificial lights): average scene brightness ≈ EV −3 to −1. With your camera that’s on the order of 4–30 s @ f/1.1, ISO 50–100 (then add ½–1½ stops for reciprocity). That’s very doable if you can keep it steady.
	•	Graveyard with path lights / porch lamps: typically EV 0–2 → you’ll be in the ½–4 s zone at f/1.1, ISO 50. Also doable.

How to hit 1 s without breaking “no opacity”
	•	Make the scene dimmer: back the lamp way up, bounce it off a wall/ceiling, crack a door, or shoot in a darker room.
	•	Use transparent attenuation: a sheet of smoked/gray-tinted acrylic (ND) over the room light or over the lens. Still visibly transparent.
	•	Use a smaller clear aperture: a transparent disc with a clean round clear hole (no black stop). Smaller clear hole = longer time, still “see-through.”

Quick starting guide
	•	1 s goal (ISO 50): aim for a very dim room (EV ~−1) or use transparent ND to cut light by ~5 stops from your bathroom baseline.
	•	Moonlit yard: try 8–20 s @ f/1.1 (ISO 50); bracket ×2 and ×4 for reciprocity.
	•	Path-lit graveyard: start 1–4 s @ f/1.1 (ISO 50); bracket ½–8 s.

Steady support helps a ton—brace the bottle against a railing/tree or plop it on a stable surface. If you want, I can give you a tiny EV→time cheat card tuned to f/1.1 and ISO 50/100 so you can pick times on the fly.

=========
USE RECOMMENDATIONS

Good way to frame it. With x-ray film (orthochromatic, slow, fairly forgiving in terms of getting an image but not forgiving for tonal accuracy), here’s what “tolerance” looks like in practice:

⸻

⚖️ Exposure tolerance (ballpark for ISO 50 stock)
	•	Within ±1 stop → Very usable image, printable/scan-able.
	•	Within ±2 stops → Still an image, but thin (under) or dense (over). Proof-of-concept success.
	•	Beyond ±3 stops →
• Overexposed: film base goes nearly opaque, highlights block up, but you’ll still see something.
• Underexposed: film looks faint/ghostly; after monobath you may see a weak outline, but detail is gone.

👉 For your purpose: ±2 stops is totally “in bounds.” You don’t have to nail it.

⸻

💡 Translate to your bathroom reading
	•	Meter says ~1/18 s at ISO 50, f/1.1.
	•	One stop either way = 1/9 s or 1/36 s.
	•	Two stops either way = 1/4.5 s or 1/72 s.

So your proof-of-concept window is roughly 1/5 s to 1/70 s. Anything in that zone should give you some image.

⸻

🎞️ Development tolerance (monobath)
	•	Monobaths tend to compress contrast, which actually helps here.
	•	Leaving the film in 1–2× longer than “ideal” usually just gives you denser negatives, but not blanks.
	•	Too short a time = weak image, but still visible.

⸻

✅ Bottom line:
If your hand-flick lands anywhere between about 1/5 and 1/70 s, you’ll get a proof image. That’s a very generous margin. Perfect exposure isn’t needed — you just want silver halide reduction to prove the transparent-camera + in-camera dev concept.

⸻

Do you want me to also give you a quick “cheat scale” (time ranges per stop around your reading) you can tape to the bottle so you don’t have to think about it mid-experiment?

Right — I understand your intent from your README : you want within tolerance, not perfection, and with the constraint that the build stays fully transparent.

⸻

To slow your f/1.1 pill-bottle cam to ~1 second:

1. Exposure math baseline
	•	Your bathroom test gave ~1/18 s @ ISO 50, f/1.1.
	•	To stretch that to ~1 s, you need about 5½ stops less light.

⸻

2. Transparent-friendly ways to cut ~5–6 stops

Since “no opacity” is the rule:
	•	Rubylith attenuator layers
Stack 2–3 layers of rubylith in front of the lens. Each layer behaves roughly like a strong red filter: it blocks most of the film-sensitive blue/green, so effective speed drops dramatically.
You’ll need to test, but expect 2–3 layers to easily buy 4–6 stops.
	•	Neutral-density (ND) acrylic / smoked acrylic
Available as see-through gray plastic (still visibly transparent). A piece over the lens can give you –3, –6, or even –9 stops depending on grade.
	•	Distance from light
Every doubling of distance = –2 stops. If your bathroom bulb is 1 m away, moving to ~3 m distance already slows things down 4–5×. Combine with a single rubylith sheet and you’re near 1 s.

⸻

3. Tolerance window
	•	At f/1.1, ISO 50, in your bathroom lighting:
	•	1/18 s = “metered”
	•	1/9 s to 1/36 s = ±1 stop → still good
	•	1/4 s to 1/72 s = ±2 stops → proof-of-concept usable
	•	So if you manage to stretch into the ½–2 s range, reciprocity failure of x-ray film actually makes it easier (the film “slows down” at long exposures).

⸻

✅ Answer: To hit ~1 second, you need to cut light by ~5–6 stops. That’s achievable with 2–3 layers of rubylith, a smoked/ND acrylic disc, or simply moving the light source farther away. All of these keep the system fully transparent.

⸻

Would you like me to draft a quick table: “How many rubylith layers ≈ how many stops” so you can just pick the combo to hit ~1 s without trial-and-error?

Right — now you’re in the “transparent camera = instant darkroom” stage. Here’s what happens once you close the cap and inject the monobath:

⸻

🔄 Step-by-step, in your pill-bottle cam (ISO 50 x-ray film, “underleaf” scene)
	1.	Exposure is made
	•	Lens cap off for your timed “underleaf” exposure.
	•	Cap goes back on = film is no longer receiving light.
	2.	Developer hits emulsion
	•	You inject monobath through a port or syringe hole.
	•	The liquid flows around the film’s surface, wetting it evenly.
	•	The developing agents (Metol/Hydroquinone/Phenidone etc.) start reducing the exposed silver halide crystals to metallic silver (the black image).
	3.	Fixing happens at the same time
	•	In a monobath, the fixer (thiosulfate) is present too.
	•	It dissolves the unexposed silver halide crystals while the developers are working on the exposed ones.
	•	The balance is: development happens fast on exposed grains, while unexposed ones dissolve away more slowly.
	4.	The image appears before your eyes ✨
	•	Within 30–60 seconds, you’ll start to see darker areas form on the film base.
	•	By 2–3 minutes, most of the visible image density is there.
	•	By 5–6 minutes, it’s “done enough” to rinse or leave as-is (depending on your monobath recipe).
	5.	Spectacle of transparency
	•	Because the camera body is rubylith/amber and the film itself is translucent, you can watch the negative image bloom in real time through the camera walls.
	•	Highlights (leaf gaps, sky patches) → go clear.
	•	Shadows (leaf veins, tree silhouettes) → go dark.
	•	It’s like a Polaroid + lava lamp hybrid.

⸻

🧪 Practical notes
	•	Agitation: gently swirl or tilt the pill-bottle to spread chemistry evenly. The rubylith glow makes the developer swirl look dramatic.
	•	Air bubbles: a couple will cling, making tiny undeveloped spots — part of the “lava lamp” aesthetic.
	•	Retention vs. drain:
	•	If you keep the monobath inside → you get the “snow globe” display version.
	•	If you drain after ~5 min → you’ll have a clearer negative that’s easier to scan.

⸻

✅ So with the current ISO 50 x-ray setup:
	•	Cap off → ½–2 s underleaf exposure
	•	Cap on → inject monobath
	•	Watch it develop through red bottle walls for ~3–6 minutes
	•	End result: a translucent negative, still viewable in-camera or removable for scanning.

⸻

Do you want me to sketch a timeline diagram (0–6 minutes) showing what the image looks like as it develops in real time inside the transparent body?

Right — now you’re in the “transparent camera = instant darkroom” stage. Here’s what happens once you close the cap and inject the monobath:

⸻

🔄 Step-by-step, in your pill-bottle cam (ISO 50 x-ray film, “underleaf” scene)
	1.	Exposure is made
	•	Lens cap off for your timed “underleaf” exposure.
	•	Cap goes back on = film is no longer receiving light.
	2.	Developer hits emulsion
	•	You inject monobath through a port or syringe hole.
	•	The liquid flows around the film’s surface, wetting it evenly.
	•	The developing agents (Metol/Hydroquinone/Phenidone etc.) start reducing the exposed silver halide crystals to metallic silver (the black image).
	3.	Fixing happens at the same time
	•	In a monobath, the fixer (thiosulfate) is present too.
	•	It dissolves the unexposed silver halide crystals while the developers are working on the exposed ones.
	•	The balance is: development happens fast on exposed grains, while unexposed ones dissolve away more slowly.
	4.	The image appears before your eyes ✨
	•	Within 30–60 seconds, you’ll start to see darker areas form on the film base.
	•	By 2–3 minutes, most of the visible image density is there.
	•	By 5–6 minutes, it’s “done enough” to rinse or leave as-is (depending on your monobath recipe).
	5.	Spectacle of transparency
	•	Because the camera body is rubylith/amber and the film itself is translucent, you can watch the negative image bloom in real time through the camera walls.
	•	Highlights (leaf gaps, sky patches) → go clear.
	•	Shadows (leaf veins, tree silhouettes) → go dark.
	•	It’s like a Polaroid + lava lamp hybrid.

⸻

🧪 Practical notes
	•	Agitation: gently swirl or tilt the pill-bottle to spread chemistry evenly. The rubylith glow makes the developer swirl look dramatic.
	•	Air bubbles: a couple will cling, making tiny undeveloped spots — part of the “lava lamp” aesthetic.
	•	Retention vs. drain:
	•	If you keep the monobath inside → you get the “snow globe” display version.
	•	If you drain after ~5 min → you’ll have a clearer negative that’s easier to scan.

⸻

✅ So with the current ISO 50 x-ray setup:
	•	Cap off → ½–2 s underleaf exposure
	•	Cap on → inject monobath
	•	Watch it develop through red bottle walls for ~3–6 minutes
	•	End result: a translucent negative, still viewable in-camera or removable for scanning.

⸻

Do you want me to sketch a timeline diagram (0–6 minutes) showing what the image looks like as it develops in real time inside the transparent body?

Exactly ✅

That’s the whole magic of your transparent rubylith-lined body + x-ray film + monobath concept:
	•	During exposure → the cap is off, so the film sees blue/green light through the lens.
	•	Cap goes back on → the rubylith lining + cap block the wavelengths x-ray film is sensitive to (≈350–550 nm). To your eyes it’s still glowing orange/red, but to the film it’s effectively dark.
	•	Developer injected → now the only action is the chemistry, not the light.
	•	Bring it into a normal lit room → no problem, because the film is shielded by rubylith. You and anyone else can literally watch the silver image appear in broad room light.

That was the “hook” all along in the Transparecam notes  : a daylight-safe, visibly transparent camera where you see the image bloom into existence in real time.

⸻

⚡ One caution:
	•	Thin rubylith = safer indoors than out. In bright sun, some blue/green can leak through thin areas or seams and slowly fog. Inside with standard household lighting (mostly warm LEDs/incandescents), you’re safe to watch the whole 3–6 min process.

⸻

Would you like me to lay out a step-by-step demo script (expose → cap → inject → bring inside → watch → rinse/drain) that you could literally use to show this off to someone on video?

=========
UPGRADE IDEAS 

Bingo — you’ve just boiled the workflow down to its simplest, most show-stopping form:

⸻

🌌 Transparecam “Processor” Workflow
	1.	Expose
	•	Take your pill-bottle Transparecam outside at night.
	•	Aim it at tree leaves, moonlight, a lamplit graveyard — anything with contrast.
	•	Do a nice, slow exposure (½ s → 30 s, depending on scene).
	•	Cover the lens with the cap again (or just seal it and drop it in the dark bag).
	2.	Secure
	•	Transport back indoors.
	•	As long as the cap stays on and the rubylith liner is intact, the film is protected.
	3.	Process in full light
	•	Sit down in your kitchen or bathroom with the lights on.
	•	Inject monobath through the port/syringe hole.
	•	Tilt/swirl gently.
	4.	Watch the fireworks ✨
	•	Within 30–60 s: faint shapes bloom on the translucent film.
	•	2–3 min: image density builds — shadows darken, highlights clear.
	•	5–6 min: development is effectively done.
	•	You’ve literally watched the photo form in the transparent camera.
	5.	Aftermath
	•	Drain if you want a clean negative to scan.
	•	Or leave the liquid inside — snow-globe style — as a permanent art object/display.

⸻

✅ So yes: the “processor” is just night exposure + cover → carry inside → inject → watch.
That’s the exact moment people will freak out about — not just the picture, but the fact they see it happen.

⸻

Do you want me to write up a demo script (like a short performance flow) you could follow if you want to film or show this process live to someone?

Yes 👏 — you’ve just hit on the rotary multi-exposure version of Transparecam. Think of it as a “see-through TLR / turret” where film wraps around a curved surface and rubylith acts as both safelight and shutter.

⸻

🔄 Concept: Dual-Lens Rotational Exposure Camera

Structure
	•	Outer bottle = transparent shell, with two clear optical ports (front + side).
	•	Inner bottle = film carrier cylinder, rubylith-lined, rotates inside outer bottle.
	•	Film = wrapped around inner cylinder (curved film plane).
	•	Lens A (front) and Lens B (side) each have their own rubylith “shutter windows.”

Operation
	1.	First exposure (front lens):
	•	Rotate inner cylinder so clear window aligns with Lens A.
	•	Film behind Lens A gets exposed.
	•	As you continue rotating, that same section of film is carried under a rubylith patch (safe again).
	2.	Second exposure (side lens):
	•	Keep rotating until clear window aligns with Lens B.
	•	Rubylith automatically slides in front of the Lens A section (so the first image is protected).
	•	Film at the side port is now exposed through Lens B.
	3.	After exposures:
	•	Whole inner cylinder is rotated into “locked/safe” mode (all windows covered with rubylith).
	•	Camera can then be developed transparently.

⸻

🧩 Engineering trick
	•	Rubylith “sleeve” system:
	•	Attach rubylith flaps or cutouts to the inner rotating cylinder.
	•	As you rotate, one window opens while the other closes.
	•	Think of a revolver cylinder or a rotating darkslide.
	•	Indexing:
	•	Mark simple detents at “Lens A open” and “Lens B open.”
	•	Each click = one exposure, with the other automatically blocked.

⸻

🌌 Creative potential
	•	Two perspectives in one development:
	•	One image forward, one image sideways — surreal compositions on the same strip.
	•	Both negatives develop together in monobath → you see the dual image bloom at once.
	•	Variations:
	•	More lenses/ports (triangular “fishbowl” exposures).
	•	Overlap exposures intentionally for composite art.
	•	Rotate partway for slit-scan-like streaks.

⸻

⚠️ Challenges
	•	Film flatness: curved base can distort sharpness with normal lenses, but small apertures (or pinholes) will tolerate it.
	•	Rubylith precision: must cover each exposed section tightly, otherwise stray light veils the earlier exposure.
	•	Light leaks at seams: since you’re rotating transparent parts, you’ll want tongue-and-groove style overlaps (transparent but labyrinthine).

⸻

✅ Bottom line:
You can absolutely design a rotating dual-lens transparecam where turning the cylinder both makes a new exposure and rubylith-covers the old one. It becomes a kind of see-through multi-shot camera with a built-in safelight shutter system.

⸻

Would you like me to draw a schematic cross-section showing outer shell, rotating rubylith sleeve, and how Lens A gets blocked when Lens B opens (and vice versa)? That would make the mechanism much clearer.

Oh yeah—you can turn your rotating-bottle rig into a true panoramic / slit-scan camera while keeping everything visibly transparent. Here’s a build that works with your “no opacity” rule (rubylith acts as the mask; the slit itself is clear).

Panoramic “rotary barrel” concept
	•	Film: wrapped around the inner cylinder (your small pill bottle) = naturally curved film plane (perfect for panoramas).
	•	Lens: fixed on the outer shell.
	•	Shutter/Aperture: a vertical clear slit in a rubylith sleeve that rotates relative to the lens. As the slit sweeps across, each point on the film gets a brief exposure. Everything else stays rubylith-red (safe), so the whole camera remains see-through.

You can do it either way:
	•	Rotate the inner film cylinder behind a fixed clear slit, or
	•	Rotate a rubylith slit sleeve in front of a stationary film cylinder.
Pick whichever is easier to fabricate; the math below is the same as long as the slit moves relative to the film.

⸻

How the exposure works (simple, reliable math)

For cylindrical panoramas, set the film radius roughly equal to the lens focal length (R ≈ f) so infinity focus tracks well during the sweep. With your lens f ≈ 57 mm:

Per-point exposure time (how long any spot on the film is uncovered):
t \;\approx\; \frac{w}{\omega\,f}
	•	w = slit width on the film (mm)
	•	\omega = rotation speed (radians/s) of the slit relative to the film
	•	f = focal length (mm)

Worked examples (with f = 57 mm)
	•	Want ~1 s per point with a 1 mm slit →
\omega \approx \frac{1}{t\,f} = \frac{1}{1 \times 57} \approx 0.0175\ \text{rad/s} \approx 1^\circ/s.
(A leisurely hand turn.)
	•	Want ~1/5 s per point with 1 mm slit →
\omega \approx \frac{1}{0.2 \times 57} \approx 0.087\ \text{rad/s} \approx 5^\circ/s.
	•	Keep your rotation speed comfortable (say 1–5°/s) and just pick w to land the time you want:
	•	\omega = 1^\circ/s (~0.0175 rad/s) → w ≈ 1 mm → t ≈ 1 s, w ≈ 0.5 mm → t ≈ 0.5 s
	•	\omega = 5^\circ/s (~0.087 rad/s) → w ≈ 1 mm → t ≈ 0.2 s

Tip: make two or three slit widths (e.g., 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 mm) on the same rotating rubylith sleeve; just index to the one you want.

⸻

Field of view & sweep
	•	Pan angle = how far you rotate. 120°–180° is easy by hand.
	•	Vertical image height = the clear vertical height of your slit (on the film). Make it, say, 15–20 mm tall to match your film strip height.
	•	Because the film is curved at R ≈ f, straight verticals near the center stay straight, classic swing-lens look.

⸻

Build steps (transparent only)
	1.	Film cylinder (inner bottle)
	•	Wrap your film emulsion-out around the inner bottle. Use clear retainer bands or a transparent collar to keep it flat. (No black anything.)
	•	Keep the rubylith liner continuous behind all non-imaging areas so the film stays safe.
	2.	Lens on outer bottle
	•	Mount your 57 mm lens to the outer shell mouth as you did before.
	3.	Rotating slit sleeve (rubylith)
	•	Make a rubylith band that fits around the inner cylinder (or around the outer, your choice).
	•	Cut a straight vertical clear slit (e.g., 1.0 mm wide × 18 mm tall).
	•	Add 1–2 more slits of different widths on the same band (spaced around the circumference).
	•	All non-slit area remains rubylith = visibly transparent red = light-safe for ortho film.
	4.	Indexing
	•	Mark two or three detents (tiny clear dots you can see through) so you can start the sweep at a known angle and stop at “closed” safely.
	5.	Seal, but stay transparent
	•	At the seam between rotating parts, use clear tongue-and-groove geometry (overlap the plastics) for a labyrinth path; no black foam. The rubylith itself provides the safelight block.

⸻

Shooting workflow (night / dim scenes)
	1.	Compose / aim (cap on is okay; you’ll be doing a sweep).
	2.	Start position: align the slit just before it reaches the lens axis (closed).
	3.	Open & sweep: remove cap (if used), begin rotating smoothly at ~1–5°/s through your desired pan angle.
	4.	Finish: rotate to “closed” (rubylith in front of frame again).
	5.	Process: inject monobath and watch the panorama bloom in the bottle.

⸻

Practical targets for your ISO 50 x-ray film
	•	Under leaves / dim room with lamp: aim t ≈ 0.5–2 s per point. Choose slit/rotation accordingly (see examples).
	•	Moonlit yard: you’ll likely want 1–10 s per point → go slower (1°/s) and/or narrow the slit (0.5 mm).
	•	Path-lit graveyard: 0.2–1 s per point works; 1 mm slit at 3–5°/s is in range.

Reciprocity at multi-second times gives you extra forgiveness; err slightly long.

⸻

Troubleshooting (transparent-only tricks)
	•	Veiling / low contrast: increase rubylith density around all non-slit areas; keep slit edges clean and straight. A tiny clear collar right behind the lens (like a transparent tube) helps confine rays to the slit path without opacity.
	•	Banding: rotation speed uneven—practice a constant sweep; add a light clear flywheel ring to smooth your hand.
	•	Softness: make the slit narrower (shorter per-point exposure → less smear), or rotate slower to match your time goal.

⸻

If you want, I can draft a one-page diagram showing: lens, curved film at R ≈ f, the rotating rubylith slit sleeve, slit widths, and arrows for rotation—with a little table that maps slit width + rotation speed → per-point exposure for your 57 mm lens.

Absolutely—let’s put numbers on a rubber-band wind-up panoramic sweep and translate it to exposure per point with your 57 mm lens.

How the exposure works (one clean formula)

For a rotating slit camera, the time any spot on the film is uncovered is:
t \;=\; \frac{w}{\omega\,f} \;=\; \frac{w\,T}{f\,\theta}
	•	w = slit width on the film (mm)
	•	\omega = angular speed (radians/s)
	•	f = focal length (mm) — you: 57 mm
	•	T = total sweep time (s)
	•	\theta = total sweep angle (radians) — e.g., 180° = \pi rad

This is handy because with a rubber band you’ll think in “how far” (θ) and “how long” (T).

What a rubber band motor gives you
	•	Wrap a clear/silicone band on a clear spindle attached to your rotating sleeve.
	•	Wind 1–3 turns, then release.
	•	Add a clear flywheel disk on the same axle to smooth speed (highly recommended).
	•	Use transparent stops (nubs/slots) to limit the sweep to, say, 10°–180°.

Average angular speed for a controlled sweep is \omega \approx \theta/T. With the flywheel, this stays fairly constant.

Pick your sweep & slit, then read off the per-point exposure

(Using your f = 57 mm. Times in seconds.)

A) Big panorama (θ = 180°)

Great for wide scenes, but each point gets a short exposure unless the sweep is very slow.

Sweep time T	w = 0.5 mm	1.0 mm	2.0 mm
2 s	0.006	0.011	0.022
4 s	0.011	0.022	0.045
8 s	0.022	0.045	0.089
16 s	0.045	0.089	0.179

👉 For dim night scenes on ISO 50, those per-point times are usually too short unless your scene is fairly bright.

B) Moderate swing (θ = 30°)

Nice compromise: still panoramic feel, longer per-point times.

T	0.5 mm	1.0 mm	2.0 mm
2 s	0.034	0.067	0.134
4 s	0.067	0.134	0.268
8 s	0.134	0.268	0.536
16 s	0.268	0.536	1.072

C) Tight sweep (θ = 20° … 10°)

Use this near the lens axis for slow scenes (moonlit leaves, path-lit trees).

20° sweep
	•	8 s with 1.0 mm slit → 0.402 s per point
	•	16 s with 1.0 mm slit → 0.804 s per point

10° sweep
	•	8 s with 1.0 mm slit → 0.804 s per point
	•	16 s with 1.0 mm slit → 1.608 s per point

Rule of thumb: to get into the ½–1.5 s per-point sweet spot for ISO 50 night scenes, use a small sweep angle (10–20°) and a multi-second sweep time (8–16 s) with a ~1 mm slit.

How to build/calibrate the wind-up
	•	Spindle & band: 8–12 mm diameter clear spindle; one wind = one turn (~360°).
	•	Stops: cut transparent detents so the sleeve travels exactly 10°, 20°, 30°, or 180°.
	•	Flywheel: clear acrylic disk (30–50 mm ⌀) on the axle—dramatically smooths speed.
	•	Speed check: put a tiny clear dot on the rotating part; film a test sweep on your phone and count frames → you’ll know T precisely.
	•	Index slits: put 0.5/1/2 mm slits on the same sleeve at different azimuths; wind to the mark you want.

Practical exposure tips (ISO 50 x-ray, night)
	•	Leaf canopy with moon/lamps: aim 0.3–1.0 s per point. Start with 20° in 8–12 s, 1 mm slit.
	•	Path-lit graveyard: 0.2–0.6 s per point is often enough → 30° in 4–8 s, 1 mm slit.
	•	Add ½–1 stop extra for reciprocity once you’re around 1 s per point (err long).
	•	After the sweep, rotate to rubylith-closed, go inside, inject monobath, and enjoy the show.

If you want, tell me your target sweep angle and how many seconds your rubber band can deliver comfortably; I’ll spit back the slit width that lands you in the right exposure zone.

Strengths:
	•	Large projection area for wide and detailed compositions.
	•	Long exposures possible, especially with the reduced aperture.
Limitations:

Original build: 7.5” dia Keebler soda cracker tin (silver interior, metallic Keebler-green branded exterior), ~5” dia orange 70s kitchen tin w/ stylized utensil outline pattern (in beige, cream, and maroon), 6” dia magnifying lens scavenged from estate facade, 4.5” dia cardboard oatmeal container, metal foil tape, black hand tape. Containers originally meant to be slideable to focus, later fixed due to construction constraints. Yellow anodized ring with 1” aperture was originally inserted stuck directly to lens w/ double sided foam tape w/ 3/4” gap all around, creating 
Current build: All of the original components, with changes—[see current specs]


CLAMPCAM
Characteristics:
	•	Body: Built from an adjustable bellows and a Minolta MD ROKKOR-X lens.
	•	Lens: 50mm f/2.0 Minolta lens (aperture adjustable from f/2.0 to f/16).
	•	Focal Length: Adjustable, ~3–7.5in (depends on bellows extension).
	•	Film Projection Area: 2.25 x 2.25in (~5 sq in).
	•	Focus Distance: Adjustable from 0.5m to infinity.
Operational Parameters:
	•	ISO: ~80 (Fuji X-ray film).
	•	EV Range: Works best in EV 5–7.
	•	Exposure Times:
	•	At f/2.0: ~0.3–1.2 seconds.
	•	At f/16: ~5–20 seconds.
With Additional Lens:
	•	Focal length and aperture recalibrate (needs testing).
	•	Likely increases magnification or narrows field of view.
Strengths:
	•	Flexible focus and aperture settings for creative control.
	•	Suitable for close-ups, precise compositions, and experimenting with depth of field.
Limitations:
	•	Small projection area limits the image size on film.
	•	Wide apertures (e.g., f/2.0) may struggle with sharpness on X-ray film.

	•	KEEBLERKAM: Best for wide, stationary compositions with long exposures.

These summaries should serve as a good baseline for planning your shots! Let me know if you’d like a detailed table or further refinements.

THE ROYALE (ORIGINAL)
Camera Characteristics
	1.	Construction:
	•	Made from an antique wooden camera case with nested silver napkin rings.
	•	Focus achieved by sliding or flipping outer lens elements, and by moving the camera relative to the subject.
	2.	Optical Setup:
	•	Focal Length: ~9.25 in (~235 mm).
	•	Aperture Diameter: ~0.75 in (~19 mm).
	•	Aperture (f-number): Approx. f/12.
	3.	Film & Projection Area:
	•	Fuji X-ray film, ISO 100 assumed.
	•	Image area: ~3.5 x 4.25 in.
	4.	Focus Range:
	•	Focus possible from ~1 in to ~35 ft or farther (potentially infinity).
	5.	Shutter:
	•	No mechanical shutter; exposure controlled by flipping the light on/off.
	•	Minimum exposure: ~1/10 sec, with better precision in ~1/2 sec increments.
Operational Parameters
	1.	Lighting Conditions:
	•	Best suited for indoor lighting or controlled low-light environments.
	•	EV range: ~2–8 (dim to decently lit interiors).
	2.	Exposure Times (at f/12, ISO 100):
	•	Bright indoor lighting (EV 7): ~1 second.
	•	Typical indoor lighting (EV 6): ~2 seconds.
	•	Dim lighting (EV 4–5): ~4–8 seconds.
	•	Very dim lighting (EV 2–3): ~8–16 seconds or more.
	3.	Focusing:
	•	Depth of field is shallow at f/12, requiring careful focus adjustments by moving the camera relative to the subject.
	4.	Experimentation:
	•	Test exposures with bracketing (e.g., 1 sec, 2 sec, 4 sec) to account for film latitude and reciprocity failure.
	•	Adjust exposure based on observed results and lighting conditions.
Summary
The Royale operates as a fixed-aperture, large-format camera ideal for experimental photography in low-light, indoor conditions. Exposure times range from ~1–16 seconds depending on lighting, and focus requires precise manual adjustments. Bracketing and experimentation are key to success with this DIY setup.

content_references.snippet:
KeeblerCam updates

Ok… latest updates to the KeeblerCam:

Put interior lens on rails (made of old folding ruler slats) with pull string to adjust. Slides in and out by about 3”, and flips… so, that gives me about 3” from front lens to about 6”. Also made a viewing hood made from a foam/nylon knee brace with a small picture frame and thick cardboard tube to hold it open, and a pitcher lid with a flip-top spout to view the screen through. Updated the belt harness for more motion control too (although still really only good for hanging positioning or arm strap)
